planting.note: Set divisions or nursery starts in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil after the threat of hard frost passes; can also be planted in early fall.

directions: Deeply lobed, almost maple-shaped dark green leaves carry bold black blotches at the center and black striping along the veins, giving the mound a smoky, near-black cast through most of the season. Slender spires of soft pink-tinged white flowers rise above the foliage in mid-spring. Forms a tight clump rather than running by stolons, making it useful for edging a shaded border without becoming invasive. Foliage color deepens further with cooler fall temperatures.

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, well-drained woodland soil in spring or early fall; keep evenly moist while establishing.

directions: One of the earliest Terra Nova foamflower introductions, with deeply cut leaves marked by a bold black star at the center that intensifies to near purple-black through winter. Coral-tinted white flower spikes emerge in spring above the clump-forming rosette. Unlike stoloniferous foamflowers, it stays compact and well-behaved, making it a reliable choice for shaded container plantings or border edges. New spring growth flushes with fresh black patterning rather than needing a season to mature into color.

planting.note: Install in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in part to full shade; a clumping selection that does not spread by runners, so space accordingly.

directions: Selected for its deeply lobed, oak-shaped bright green leaves and notable resistance to summer heat and humidity compared with straight species foamflower. New growth emerges with a bronze cast in spring and foliage picks up red tones again in autumn. Wiry stems carry light pink buds that open to tiny white bottlebrush flowers well above the mound. A tidy clumper rather than a stoloniferous spreader, it suits woodland border fronts and shaded rock gardens where a running groundcover would be unwelcome.

planting.note: Set out divisions in rich, moisture-retentive soil in part to full shade during cool spring or fall weather.

directions: Named for foliage lobes fancifully likened to a swan in flight, this Terra Nova selection has deeply cut green leaves etched with contrasting black veining. Wiry, mostly leafless flower stems rise well above the foliage mound in mid-spring, carrying dense bottlebrush racemes of fragrant pink-tinged white flowers. Forms a dense, clump-forming mound that holds its patterned foliage through the growing season. Effective massed as a shaded groundcover or tucked into a woodland border where its dissected leaf shape reads as a distinct texture next to broader-leaved companions.

planting.note: Plant divisions in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in part to full shade; give it room to form a full mound over two to three seasons.

directions: Distinguished from the many silver-patterned brunneras by its large, heart-shaped leaves in a bright yellow-green that brightens deeply shaded corners without any variegation. Airy sprays of small, lightly fragrant true-blue forget-me-not flowers rise above the foliage in mid-spring. Leaf color is most vivid in cooler weather and can soften toward green as summer heat arrives, especially with insufficient shade. Works well as a chartreuse foil for the silver- and white-marked brunnera cultivars and other dark-leaved shade companions.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or fall into humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist through summer; avoid overhead watering to reduce mildew.

directions: One of the earliest lungworts bred for nearly solid-silver foliage, with so much silver speckling that the spots merge and leave only a thin green margin around each leaf. Clusters of magenta buds open pink and mature to blue, giving a two-tone bloom effect typical of the genus in early spring. An Adrian Bloom introduction that helped launch the modern wave of all-silver pulmonaria breeding, though it can be prone to occasional reversion to plainer foliage. Best in a cool, humus-rich site where the luminous leaves can be appreciated through summer and fall.

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, moisture-retentive soil in part to full shade in early spring or fall.

directions: A compact, mildew-resistant selection with narrow green leaves so heavily splashed with silver that the frosted patches often outweigh the green background. Soft rose-pink flower clusters open in very early spring and gradually fade to violet-blue as they age, creating a bicolor display on the same plant. Its tidy, dense habit makes it useful for the front of a shaded border or as a small-scale groundcover, in contrast to the broader-leaved saccharata types. Foliage remains attractive and largely spot-free of mildew through summer heat.

planting.note: Set divisions into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in part shade during cool spring or fall weather.

directions: A Dan Heims hybrid combining the parentage of 'Bertram Anderson' and angustifolia 'Azurea', producing narrow, silver-spotted lance-shaped leaves finer in texture than most saccharata-type lungworts. Giant cobalt-blue flowers open in very early spring and continue for weeks longer than typical pulmonaria bloom. Its compact, mildew-resistant mound stays low and tidy, making it well suited to the front of a shaded bed or tucked among ferns and hellebores. Flower color is notably deeper and more saturated than many blue-flowered lungwort cultivars.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in well-drained soil in part shade with some sun; space to allow the mat to knit together over one growing season.

directions: One of the older, still widely grown bugleweed selections, forming a dense, glossy mat of spoon-shaped leaves in a deep bronze-purple that deepens further in cool weather. Short, erect spikes of vivid deep blue flowers stud the mat in late spring, drawing bees heavily. Leaf color develops best with some direct sun rather than deep shade, distinguishing it from purely shade-grown groundcovers. A vigorous spreader by stolons, useful for quickly covering bare ground or suppressing weeds beneath shrubs, though it can need edging to control its spread.

planting.note: Set plugs or divisions into well-drained soil in shade to part sun; establishes quickly as a low evergreen mat.

directions: Forms tight rosettes of rounded, gray-green leaves crinkled in texture and heavily mottled with creamy white, giving the mat a frosted, dusty appearance distinct from the darker bronze bugleweed cultivars. Foliage shifts toward burgundy tones as temperatures drop in fall, adding cool-season interest. Medium-blue flower spikes stand several inches above the variegated carpet in spring, drawing pollinators. Tolerant of both shade and considerable sun, it makes a low, drought-tolerant, deer-resistant groundcover for edging paths or filling gaps between stepping stones.

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; slow to spread compared with typical bugleweed, so space plants closer together for quicker coverage.

directions: A Chris Hansen introduction in the Feathered Friends series, bred from a cross between clumping Ajuga tenorei and running Ajuga reptans, resulting in a much slower, non-invasive spreader than typical bugleweed. Crinkled, ruffled foliage emerges bronze and matures to gold, giving a warm two-tone color shift across the patch through the season. Spikes of small violet-blue flowers appear in spring above the textured evergreen mat. Its restrained spread makes it a better-behaved choice than most Ajuga reptans cultivars for small beds or mixed containers where an aggressive groundcover would be unwelcome.
